newsitem.title: BELGIUM: New Belgian scandal puts sex offences in spotlight.
newsitem.headline: New Belgian scandal puts sex offences in spotlight.

text.p: Belgium must urgently review the way it deals with sex offenders, authorities said on Thursday following the discovery of the remains of a nine-year old child who went missing five years ago.
Late on Wednesday Belgian investigators found the decomposed body of a child, tentatively identified as Moroccan-born Loubna Benaissa, in a steel trunk under a Brussels garage.
Police arrested the petrol-pump attendant, a 33-year-old convicted sex offender who lived less than a mile away from the girl in the capital's Ixelles district. They also held three others.

"This drama is another stimulus for the government to continue its justice reform programme, notably a review of the treatment of convicted sex offenders and the reform of the law of conditional release," Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene said in a statement on Thursday.
"We have to speed up the review of the entire system for punishment of sexual delinquency," Justime Minister Stefaan De Clerck told RTBF television.

The justice reform programme was started last year, after the discovery of the bodies of two little girls and two teenagers in August. Convicted child rapist Marc Dutroux has been charged with their murder.
Dutroux was released for good behaviour in 1992 after serving only three years of a 13-year sentence for multiple child rape.
Belgian media said the suspect held in Loubna's case had been convicted and jailed in 1984 for sexual assault of three young children.
He spent less than two months in jail in 1984, and the police closed his dossier in March 1992, only months before Loubna, then nine years old, disappeared in August.

"A new draft law contains measures for sexual delinquents, who will receive special guidance during and after their punishment, and who may have to remain in custody, even after their jail sentence, if there is a risk of repeat offence," Dehaene's statement said.
An April 1995 law already calls for a treatment and guidance plan for released sex offenders, but specialists say that there are not enough specialist centres to fill that need.
"The existing facilities do not suffice to fill the need," Paul Cosyns, Antwerp University psychiatrist and head of the UFC sex offence treatment centre, told Reuters.
The UFC has about 110 sex offenders or sexual delinquents under treatment. Cosyns could not say how many sex offenders currently are free and how many enjoy special guidance.
There are some 8,000 people in jail in Belgium, of whom 11 percent were convicted of sex crimes, he said.
Ibrahim Bouhna of the Brussels mosque who gave counselling to the Benaissa family last night told Reuters that sex offenders should be removed from society.

"It is dramatic that the offender did not receive adequate guidance. But the question is how long someone can be put under surveillance. In Islam, we think that society should be protected from perverted people by keeping them removed from society," he said.
Belgian child rights activist Marie-France Botte also called for closer follow-up of child sex offenders.
"Paedophilia can be treated succesfully in about 50 percent of cases, but it has to be done in jail. However, once a paedophile has killed, he is untreatable," she told Reuters.
But UFC psychologist Dirk De Doncker said paedophilia at any level was basically untreatable.

"We do not have the impression that we can change sexual preferences. A paedophile remains a paedophile. We can help them change the way in which they deal with their urge, but we cannot change the urge itself," he said.
